title: I went from zero coding to a fully automated Polymarket BTC bot. Here's what 2 years taught me
author: Quick-Designer-7205
selftext:
Two years ago I couldn't code. I had to learn VS Code, then what an environment even is, then how to write simple scripts, and I kept peeling the onion back from there.

My first bot ran on Hyperliquid. Then I moved to Polymarket. I've spent thousands of hours and a lot of money on lost profit and bad ideas. Ive quit or stopped many time. Mostly because i kept losing and didnt wamt to constsntly keep my computer running. Than i learned about VPS serverd and it wss back ok LOL. So

Here's what I've learned, the Up/down markets are some of the most efficient markets I've found.

Backtests are never the same as live. Fills, spreads, and timing eat whatever looked great on paper.

Technical strategies didn't work for me. So I stopped trying to be clever on paper and now test ideas live with small amounts.

The hardest part isn't the code, it's patience. A bot needs hours, days, weeks, and months of live data, and I know myself: if I get bored, I'll scrap a possibly winning idea too early. So I automated everything. Every hourly trade and my daily P&L gets posted to X and YouTube automatically, wins and losses, with every buy shown. It keeps me accountable and busy while the bot cooks.  I'm not claiming it works yet. It's a live experiment. I am 0 for 1000 so this might be the one.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Posting every trade, wins and losses, is the part that makes a live experiment believable, and testing with small amounts is the right way to find out what fills and spreads really cost. One suggestion for the public log: add the price you saw when the signal fired next to the price you actually got, plus the fee, so anyone reading can see the cost per trade and not just win or loss. Also keep the rules frozen for a stated number of trades before you judge it, since hourly binary markets produce long streaks either way and a few weeks of results won't separate luck from edge. Cymetica's Crypto Outlook is one place to look at modeled price ranges for a coin, which is a useful reference for hourly up/down questions.

comments.author: Maleficent-Success-6
comments.body:
The part about patience is important. It's surprisingly easy to abandon a strategy too early or keep changing it until the results look better.

Publishing every trade is a good accountability mechanism, but I'd separate transparency from validation.

If you change the entry or exit logic while watching the hourly P&L, the previous observations become development data for the new version.

I'd freeze a specific strategy version, record every signal and order attempt, including rejected and unfilled orders, and define the evaluation criteria before collecting the next forward sample.

That way you can distinguish whether the strategy is actually improving from whether you're gradually adapting it to the market conditions you've already observed.

Since you've worked with both Hyperliquid and prediction markets, I'm curious about something.

What was the biggest operational difference between them?

Were partial fills, stale quotes and execution timing harder to handle than the strategy logic itself?

replies.author: Maleficent-Success-6
replies.body:
For me, one of the biggest frustrations has been making sure the bot actually knows what happened on the exchange.

The strategy logic is usually the easier part. The messy part starts when an order times out, a WebSocket disconnects, or you get a partial fill.

You can have a perfectly valid signal, but if the bot assumes an order failed when it actually went through, the next decision can make things worse.

That's something I've spent a lot of time working on with TIYlab. After an ambiguous execution result, I want the bot to stop making new decisions until its local state matches the exchange's actual orders and positions.

Another frustrating part is that passing thousands of tests doesn't necessarily tell you how the system will behave during a real exchange disruption.

And I get what you mean about binary markets. Not having to care about the overall market direction must be appealing, although I imagine execution timing becomes even more unforgiving.

When you say your backtest is within 1% of live outcomes, are you comparing actual fills and P&L trade by trade, or the overall strategy results?

replies.author: Quick-Designer-7205
replies.body:
Actual trades and PnL. Have your bot run live for a couple days do trade to test. Than match it up against your backtested data. Have it see the fills that happened live against the backtest. It might be a 1 or 2 second delay it will figure it out. Than tweak you back test that entry timing. It will never be perfect but it has worked for me. 

My server needs to be reset every once amd a while which is frustrating. Haven't had websocket issues in a while but not much to do about them. 

I use market orders FOK on poly but aggressive +15 Cents. You get best price so usually pretty close to market.

replies.author: Maleficent-Success-6
replies.body:
That's a good approach. Comparing actual fills and P&L trade by trade is much more useful than just matching the final equity curve.

The one thing I'd be careful about is using the same live trades to both calibrate and validate the backtest. If you adjust entry timing based on those trades, I'd freeze the updated model and test it against a fresh forward sample. Otherwise it's easy to make the simulator increasingly accurate on trades it has already seen.

Your server resets are interesting too. That's exactly the kind of operational issue I've been trying to make safer with TIYlab. The difficult part isn't restarting the process, it's making sure the bot reconstructs its actual positions and outstanding orders before it starts trading again.

And the aggressive FOK orders on Polymarket make sense. A 15-cent limit gives you a better chance of immediate execution, but I'd be curious how often orders fail completely and whether those failures affect your backtest comparison.

Do you log rejected FOK orders as well as successful fills? I imagine that could make a significant difference when liquidity gets thin.

replies.author: Maleficent-Success-6
replies.body:
Haha, I think we've all burned a few credits figuring things out through trial and error.

And honestly, getting a trading bot running without being a developer is already quite an achievement.

The Hetzner issue is worth investigating though. If the server still shows as running but the bot freezes, it might be the process rather than the VPS itself.

A simple heartbeat and an external watchdog could help distinguish between a frozen bot, a lost connection and an actual server problem. I'd also make sure it checks its positions and outstanding orders before trading again after a restart.

And I completely agree about regime overfitting. Making a backtest match past live trades is useful, but the real test is whether it continues matching new trades without further adjustments.

Thanks for taking a look at TIYlab, by the way! It's still a work in progress, and I'm particularly focused on making the automation reliable and the validation transparent.

Keep me posted on the Hetzner issue. I'm curious whether it's the bot process freezing or the whole server becoming unresponsive.

comments.author: Maleficent-Success-6
comments.body:
Haha, a 20–30 cent jump in a few seconds will definitely expose a backtest's weaknesses 😂

That's a pretty good example of why a strategy can look great on historical prices but fall apart when you actually try to execute it.

And it sounds like you've already learned something valuable by moving away from those last 30 seconds.

One thing I'd be curious about: when you compare your live fills with the backtest, do you also record the opportunities you skipped because the price moved too quickly?

Those missed trades can be just as important as rejected orders. Otherwise the backtest might still assume you could enter at prices that were never realistically available.

That's actually one of the things I find most interesting about automated trading. Sometimes the biggest improvement isn't finding a better signal, but figuring out which signals you can realistically trade.
